qt: to the Commission Christine Anderson (ID) Subject:

The planned closure of the Goodyear factory in Fulda1 is a stark reminder of the challenges faced by industry and the economy as a result of the European Green Deal. ‘Fulda tyres’ will no longer be manufactured in Fulda. Instead, they will be manufactured elsewhere but still be sold under the same name, despite the fact that after 2025 there will be no tyre factory in Fulda anymore. 1.

Given the high industrial electricity costs in Germany (13-15 cent per kilowatt hour) compared to the US (4 cent) and Asia (1.5 cent), how does the Commission assess the European Green Deal’s impact on the competitiveness of energy-intensive businesses in the EU and their relocation outside the Union?

What steps is the Commission taking to address job losses in traditional, energy-intensive industries, and to what extent will the sectors supported by the European Green Deal be able to compensate for these losses without having to rely on subsidies in the long term?

Would it be possible to recognise and protect the ‘Fulda tyres’ brand as a designation of origin in order to highlight and possibly preserve the regional and cultural significance of the Fulda factory?
at: (English version) to the Commission Christine Anderson (ID) (20 March 2024) Subject: Closure of the Goodyear tyre factory in Fulda — energy cost challenges — saving jobs in the context of the European Green Deal The planned closure of the Goodyear factory in Fulda (1) is a stark reminder of the challenges faced by industry and the economy as a result of the European Green Deal. ‘Fulda tyres’ will no longer be manufactured in Fulda. Instead, they will be manufactured elsewhere but still be sold under the same name, despite the fact that after 2025 there will be no tyre factory in Fulda anymore. 1. Given the high industrial electricity costs in Germany (13-15 cent per kilowatt hour) compared to the US (4 cent) and Asia (1.5 cent), how does the Commission assess the European Green Deal’s impact on the competitiveness of energy-intensive businesses in the EU and their relocation outside the Union? 2. What steps is the Commission taking to address job losses in traditional, energy-intensive industries, and to what extent will the sectors supported by the European Green Deal be able to compensate for these losses without having to rely on subsidies in the long term? 3. Would it be possible to recognise and protect the ‘Fulda tyres’ brand as a designation of origin in order to highlight and possibly preserve the regional and cultural significance of the Fulda factory? (1 July 2024) The European Green Deal is Europe’s green growth strategy. The green transition is necessary to mitigate and adapt to the urgent climate crisis and is expected to create between 1 and 2.5 million additional net jobs in the EU (2), even if leading to job losses in certain sectors and regions. Energy intensive industries play an essential role in the achievement of the green, digital and resilience objectives of the EU. The Commission is working to ensure that such activities can prosper and remain competitive in the EU, with several EU instruments available for assistance for energy-intensive manufacturing sectors (3) in particular. The clean energy transition can contribute to boosting competitiveness and strategic autonomy, by phasing out dependence on expensive and volatile fossil fuels imports from unreliable partners and by ensuring that energy price levels are better aligned with the needs of domestic and industrial end-users. Geographical indication protection for craft and industrial products as established by the 2023 Regulatio n (4) aims to improve awareness as regards the authenticity of products and safeguard cultural heritage. Product names like ‘Fulda tyres’ may be eligible for protection if they comply with the necessary requirements. It will be possible to apply for geographical indication protection as from 1 December 2025 (5).
